title: Daily cross (Luke 9:18–27)
hook: Luke adds one word: take up your cross daily

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve sent out, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was you give them something to eat. What did your skipped comfort become for someone else? Day five hundred thirty-five.

Matthew, Mark and Luke all record the same hard saying: if anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself and take up his cross. But Luke's version has one extra word. Just one. It is easy to miss, and once you see it, the whole sentence changes shape. It comes right after a quiet moment. Luke says Jesus was "alone praying," with only his disciples nearby. Again, prayer at a turning point. And when he finishes, he asks them a question, the kind you'd ask your closest friends late at night when the crowd has gone home: "Whom say the people that I am?"
screen: `WHOM SAY THE PEOPLE THAT I AM?`

segments.voice: They report the gossip: some say John the Baptist, back from the dead; others Elijah; others one of the old prophets. Then he makes it personal: "But whom say ye that I am?" And Peter answers: "The Christ of God." Christ means anointed one, the Messiah, the king Israel hoped for. And immediately Jesus tells them not to spread it, and says something nobody expected a Messiah to say: "The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and be raised the third day." Then, to everyone: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." There it is. Daily. In Greek, kath hemeran, day by day. Matthew and Mark don't have it. In Rome's world, a cross wasn't a symbol. It was how the empire executed rebels and slaves, and the condemned man carried the crossbeam himself through the streets. Taking up your cross meant walking toward the end. Matthew and Mark say it like a single great decision. Luke adds daily, and the picture shifts: not one dramatic moment, but a thing you pick up again every morning. Christians across the centuries have heard it both ways at once. Some have literally faced death for their faith. Most have faced the ordinary kind: putting someone else first again today, keeping a promise again today, not getting their own way again today. "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it." In Luke, losing your life happens one day at a time.
screen: `WHOM SAY YE? THE CHRIST OF GOD.`
then, large: `TAKE UP HIS CROSS DAILY, AND FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one daily faithful thing. Settle, and breathe. Think about the ordinary weight you carry every day, the thing that's yours to pick up whether you feel like it or not. Caring for a parent. Showing up to a job that's hard. Being patient with a child, or with your own body. Staying honest when no one would know. Don't make it bigger than it is, and don't make it smaller. Just see it. Then picture tomorrow morning, picking it up again, on purpose this time, not grudgingly. Imagine doing it with a little love in it. If you pray, you can offer that daily weight to God. If you don't, simply choose to carry it with care. The bell holds the time.
Daily cross. Peter names Jesus the Christ of God, and Jesus says anyone who follows him must take up the cross, and Luke adds the word daily.
Your line: daily. Tomorrow morning, before anything else, pick up your ordinary weight on purpose. And today, carry it one more time with care. Day five hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians speak of "carrying their cross" for the ordinary burdens of daily life, and in many traditions the daily offering of one's day to God is a morning practice.

fork.setup: Jesus asks his closest friends: but who do you say that I am? you're Peter. what do you say?
fork.reveal: Peter says the Christ of God. and Jesus answers that the Son of man must suffer, and that following him means a cross taken up daily.

original.note: Greek: day by day, daily. the word only Luke adds to "take up his cross."

trapdoor: what you thought: "take up your cross" means one heroic sacrifice.
what it means: Luke adds daily, so the cross becomes something picked up again every morning, in ordinary faithfulness.
what a scholar hears: Matthew 16:24 and Mark 8:34 lack kath hemeran; Luke's addition turns a once-for-all call into a daily rhythm.

notes: kath hemeran in Luke 9:23 (a few manuscripts lack it). Confirm.
Roman crucifixion and the condemned carrying the crossbeam (patibulum): standard history. Rome executed Jesus; the script quotes 9:22's list of those who reject him without blame framing.
Hook says the extra word is easy to miss (no claim about most readers).
